I just wrote a 600 word blog post but I pressed paste instead of copy, then accidentally deleted it all. Im upset. But what’s more upsetting was how BORING THIS MOVIE WAS. It was an absolute Snoozefest. I don’t understand how so many people like this movie and how it was culturally impactful at all. This movie was an absolute time waster, just so happy to waste your time. That intro? so insanely long for what? To create suspense? if the scene needs 10 minutes of people doing nothing in order to build suspense, then i’m sorry, you’re not good at building suspense. 30 minutes into the movie almost nothing of substance happens, and one hour into the movie the plot has just barely been introduced and begun. That sucks. If your movie needs that much backstory to get it started, maybe you should’ve split it into two parts. But that’s the thing, this movie doesn’t need that much backstory. There is truly no reason at all for this movie to be three hours long. Like at all. This story could’ve been told in an hour 25 I promise you. And that would’ve probably made it more entertaining. But it’s hard to say, cause it was so hard for me to pay attention to the film. There was nothing for me to latch onto. The story felt all over the place, so many scenes went on for way too long, and none of the characters were likable! I will say this, Jills and hair and makeup were absolutely incredible. Her eyelashes were always dark and Lucious, and her hair was always moisturized and shiny. But besides that, there is literally nothing likable about any of these characters. They’re all so nasty, mean, and stoic. There is not an ounce of emotion in this movie it seems. So the plot is boring and takes forever, and the characters are unlikeable, now what. What do you have left for your movie? Is it visually appealing? absolutely not. are there lots of spectacle or impressive stunts? not really. So this movie has almost nothing to offer. The genre, time period, budget, and movie length are not excuses for why this movie was so boring. Dances with Wolves is a perfect example of this. Dances With Wolves is 3 hours of a beautiful, touching, human story. With characters you can grow with and root for. And there are westerns made before Once Upon A Time that do a much better and more efficient job of storytelling. For example, High Noon. High Noon does not drag even for a second, there is lots of emotion and suspense OHHH THE SUSPENSE!!! And the movie is fully entertaining and takes just the right amount of time. Also it’s very beautiful to watch. There are really no excuses for this movie to be as unentertaining as it was. But also, personally, I don’t feel like this was a story worth telling. Especially if you’re telling it for three hours omg. A bunch of people fighting for a plot of land, okay cool. There’s a woman who used to be a prostitute, a guy with a harmonica, and a guy on a train with a broken neck, how invigorating. This movie is just such a nothing burger to me. The reason why people praise it so much probably lies in the historical context and post production aspects of it, cause surely it can’t be the movie itself. I really can’t think of anything good to say about this movie, I just don’t get it. It feels like an obnoxious, self indulgent, movie that doesn’t even want most audience goers to enjoy it. I feel a sense of whoever made it thinking his story was soooo good that it absolutely deserved to take 3 hours, and if you can’t sit through all the BS scenes that take forever to get anywhere, then you just don’t get real art. But that’s just me, I don’t know anything about whoever made the movie and why they did it. The movie just takes itself so seriously it feels pretentious to me. cause surely you know most people will get bored and have trouble keeping their attention. Surely you knew that!!! so then why’d you make it? I don’t feel like this story is artsy enough to be only for the sophisticated cinephile, but it’s not entertaining enough for the average movie-goer. I seriously don’t like this movie at all.

I understand that Sergio Leone’s Once Upon a Time in the West is celebrated for its deliberate storytelling, atmospheric tension and distinctive approach to the western genre. But I genuinely cannot understand how anyone could expect me to remain invested in a movie that moves at such an agonizingly slow pace. Every movement feels prolonged, every conversation unfolds as though the characters have all the time in the world, and practically every scene seems determined to stretch itself beyond what I consider remotely necessary. And the opening sequence alone perfectly illustrates my frustration. We spend what feels like an eternity watching three gunmen arrive at a railway station, position themselves and do practically nothing while waiting for a train. The camera dedicates an extraordinary amount of attention to their smallest movements, the surrounding silence and seemingly insignificant details. At one point, we spend several minutes watching a man become increasingly annoyed by a fly, which he eventually manages to trap inside the barrel of his revolver. Seriously? I understand the intention to create anticipation through silence, prolonged observation and minute details, but I found it almost comically tedious. We are barely into the movie, and I am already wondering how much longer I am supposed to watch people stand around before something actually happens. The sequence eventually develops into a confrontation, but by then my patience has already been thoroughly tested. And unfortunately, that opening establishes the rhythm of practically everything that follows. The pacing is absolutely unbearable. Everyone walks in slow motion, everyone talks in slow motion, and even the simplest interactions seem to require an extraordinary amount of patience. I recognize the intention to build anticipation through prolonged silences, calculated movements and carefully constructed confrontations, but that approach did absolutely nothing for me. Rather than becoming increasingly absorbed in the atmosphere, I found myself growing progressively more frustrated with the sheer amount of time required for anything meaningful to happen. The characters were not particularly compelling either. Their motivations and conflicts offer some dramatic substance, but I struggled to develop any meaningful attachment to them. The dialogue is unnecessarily drawn out, the narrative progression feels painfully sluggish, and whatever tension the movie attempts to establish is repeatedly undermined by its insistence on taking the longest possible route toward every development. I can appreciate certain aspects of the production. The western environments, costumes and carefully composed imagery demonstrate an obvious commitment to the setting, while the camerawork occasionally produces some interesting visual moments. But I found the overall presentation considerably less impressive than its reputation suggests, particularly when the editing and pacing make even potentially exciting confrontations feel unnecessarily exhausting. My problem is not that Once Upon a Time in the West refuses to rush. I have enjoyed plenty of deliberately paced movies when their restraint contributes to compelling storytelling. Here, however, I found almost no enjoyment in the experience. The prolonged stares, extended pauses and painfully measured interactions eventually became so monotonous that I struggled to care about the outcome of the story. And with a runtime approaching three hours, that frustration only becomes more pronounced. I have no objection to lengthy movies when their narratives provide enough substance, complexity or emotional engagement to justify the additional time. But here, so much of that runtime seems dedicated to stretching moments that could have communicated their purpose in a fraction of the time. Even the smallest gestures are treated as events deserving prolonged observation, and I simply did not find that approach rewarding. Originality: 5 Complexity: 4 Emotional Depth: 3 Impact & Inspiration: 1 Characters: 4 Performance: 5 Dialogue: 3 Line Delivery: 5 Score: 4 Sound Design: 4 Production Design: 5 Camerawork: 5 Editing: 3 Pacing: 1 Engagement: 2 Entertainment: 2 Narrative Discipline: 3 Cinematography: 5 Rewatchability: 1 Overall Rating: 3.4/10 Once Upon a Time in the West is an extraordinarily frustrating experience whose deliberate pacing completely destroyed whatever interest I might have developed in its characters and story. I can acknowledge the craftsmanship behind its production and understand why some viewers admire Leone’s patient approach to building atmosphere, but I found that patience almost impossible to appreciate. The opening railway station sequence perfectly captures everything that eventually exhausted me about the movie: an extraordinary amount of time devoted to minimal activity, presented with such exaggerated restraint that I struggled to find any meaningful tension beneath it. Every conversation, movement and confrontation seems to unfold at a fraction of the speed I would have preferred, turning what could have been a compelling western into a painfully prolonged exercise in endurance. I have no objection to a movie taking its time, but I expect that time to reward my attention. Unfortunately, this one seemed determined to test how much of it I was willing to surrender.

I really struggled to finish this one. Westerns are just not my thing, and this movie made that very clear. I just don’t see the appeal. While I can understand the nostalgia people can project onto western stories, I just don’t feel entertained by 2 hours and 45 minutes of boring people in boring places talking about boring things. That may sound very one-dimensional and short-sighted, but that is exactly what bothers me about this film and probably also about all other movies of this kind. Just because something is old and slow-paced does not automatically make it good. It is not a complete disaster, because some of the cringey dialogue did entertain me, and the music was also used quite well in some moments (but definitely not all of them!). The third aspect I kinda enjoyed was some of the wide shots and the production design. But when every person in this film is basically the same (old man with a dirty face, cowboy hat on, mumbling something) then it just bores me to death. I don’t care if it is considered a classic or not.

I feel like Leone is all style and no design. Other films can succeed with narrative vacuums, wherein the caesuras are integral to the aesthetic pressure - as in daft punk does in electroma or Tarkovsky does in stalker. But in the large narrative deserts between the few interesting events of a movie like West , no intellectual or psychological atmosphere permeates. It's dead, dry air. You genuinely feel like your time is being wasted, especially when decides to "build tension" via making you a sequence 5x longer than it needs to be... it's really only slick compositions and epic chord progressions that keeps you seated. Compared to The Good, The Bad & The Ugly , West Feels alot better styled, in that its commited harder to the desolation. The empty writing doesn't feel as out of place and can more convincingly feign ideological design. But its still utterly understimulating.

Overrated as F.  Sergio Leone directs as though every glance deserves its own memorial service. A man waits for a train, another man stares across a dusty street, someone reaches for a gun—each moment stretched until it begins to feel less like suspense than a test of endurance. The film seems convinced that because it is taking its time, it must be saying something profound. Sometimes it's simply taking its time. Henry Fonda is the exception. Casting America's most decent face as a killer was a marvelous piece of intuition, and he gives the movie a cold, unsettling gravity whenever he appears. He has the confidence to underplay, which makes everyone else's myth-making seem all the more self-conscious. When Fonda is on screen, the movie briefly remembers that performances can create tension more effectively than endless close-ups of squinting eyes and weathered faces. Leone's visual style is undeniably handsome, but after a while the film becomes infatuated with itself. Every scene strains to be iconic before it has earned the right. Every silence insists upon its own importance. You begin to feel the director nudging your elbow: *Isn't this magnificent?* Not especially. Sometimes a western should simply saddle up and move. The strange thing is how its reputation has inflated over the decades. During the 1970s, when American cinema was exploding with genuinely daring work—from *The Godfather* to *Chinatown*, *Nashville*, *The Conversation*, and dozens more—few people were treating *Once Upon a Time in the West* as the untouchable masterpiece it is now often declared to be. Its modern canonization says as much about changing critical fashions as it does about the movie itself. Nor is it the finest film of 1968. That year alone offered richer, bolder achievements in entirely different directions. It isn't the greatest western, either. And despite Fonda's excellent work, it isn't even the best western in which Henry Fonda appeared. His career contains leaner, sharper pictures that understand an old truth: a western doesn't become epic because it lasts nearly three hours. It becomes epic because every scene matters. There are pleasures here—the score, Fonda's deliciously icy villain, and Leone's gift for composition—but they're buried beneath a mountain of cinematic self-importance. Admire it if you like. Revere it if you must. Just don't confuse slowness with depth or length with greatness.

me pareció una película excelente aunque entiendo que su ritmo lento puede hacer que no sea para todo el mundo, es un western bastante diferente a los más convencionales porque se toma mucho tiempo para construir la atmósfera, presentar a los personajes y aumentar la tensión lo que más me gustó fue la dirección de sergio leone, hay escenas en las que prácticamente no ocurre nada pero la forma en que utiliza los silencios, los primeros planos y la música consigue que igualmente estés esperando a ver qué va a pasar la escena inicial en la estación es un buen ejemplo: es larguísima y aparentemente sencilla pero termina siendo una de las partes más tensas de toda la película la música de ennio morricone también me pareció espectacular, creo que tiene un papel fundamental y que algunas escenas no tendrían el mismo impacto sin ella, cada personaje tiene una identidad musical bastante marcada y eso ayuda mucho a crear la sensación de que estamos viendo algo casi mítico charles bronson como harmonica me gustó mucho, es un protagonista bastante misterioso y durante buena parte de la película no sabes exactamente cuales son sus intenciones henry fonda también me sorprendió muchísimo interpretando a frank, estamos acostumbrados a verlo en papeles más heroicos y acá hace justamente lo contrario: un personaje frío y despiadado y creo que ese contraste funciona muy bien claudia cardinale también me pareció muy buena como jill, me gustó que su personaje tuviera bastante más importancia de la que suele tener la protagonista femenina en muchos westerns de la época, ella es una de las personas que realmente tiene algo que perder y termina siendo fundamental para el conflicto lo que menos me gustó fue precisamente el ritmo: la película dura bastante y hay momentos en los que sentí que algunas escenas podrían haber sido más cortas, leone disfruta muchísimo de los silencios y de alargar ciertos momentos y aunque eso funciona muy bien para crear tensión también puede resultar pesado si no conectas con ese estilo además, la historia no es especialmente compleja pero está contada de una manera que exige bastante paciencia, no creo que sea una película para poner de fondo mientras haces otra cosa porque gran parte de su atractivo está precisamente en observar los detalles y dejar que las escenas se desarrollen aún así, creo que es una de esas películas en las que el estilo termina siendo tan importante como la propia historia: los paisajes, los encuadres, la música y los personajes hacen que tenga una personalidad enorme se siente como una despedida de una época del western y al mismo tiempo como una película que intenta convertir a sus personajes en figuras casi legendarias

Spiel mir das Lied vom Tod überzeugt vor allem mit seiner großartigen Western-Atmosphäre. Die staubigen Schauplätze, die beeindruckenden Landschaftsaufnahmen und das aufwendige Set-Design sorgen dafür, dass man komplett in die Welt des Wilden Westens eintaucht. Besonders hervorzuheben ist die legendäre Filmmusik von Ennio Morricone, die den Film durchgehend trägt und viele Szenen noch eindrucksvoller macht. Auch die Kameraarbeit mit ihren ikonischen Nahaufnahmen und die starke Präsenz der Hauptfiguren machen den Film visuell sehr sehenswert. Leider wird der Film seinem Ruf für mich nicht ganz gerecht. Das größte Problem ist das extrem langsame Erzähltempo. Viele Szenen ziehen sich unnötig in die Länge, wodurch immer wieder Spannung verloren geht. Zwar sollen die langen Einstellungen Atmosphäre aufbauen, für mich wirkte das aber oft eher zäh als packend. Auch die Handlung entwickelt sich über weite Strecken nur schleppend, sodass der Film trotz seiner starken Inszenierung nie ä mitreißend wurde. Insgesamt ist Spiel mir das Lied vom Tod zweifellos ein stilprägender Western mit großartiger Musik, beeindruckenden Bildern und einigen unvergesslichen Szenen. Das sehr gemächliche Tempo hat den Film für mich jedoch deutlich ausgebremst. Deshalb reicht es am Ende nur für 2,5 von 5 Sternen.

I don’t know how it happened, but over the last couple of years the western has become one of my favorite film genres. I used to be a Cool Guy who liked Bergman and Sydow. Fellini and Mastroianni*. But now I like John Ford and John Wayne. Budd Boetticher and Randolph Scott. Laaame. And what I like about these films is that, on the surface, they’re pretty straightforward. Classic Hollywood storytelling. That’s what I like. I’m a simple man. But behind that simplicity there’s a simmering feeling. It’s all a facade. It’s myth-making. In a way, it’s a genre made to completely whitewash and sanitize history. American history. And that’s why the western is such a specifically American genre. It’s the only place it could be born. Every American western is a reckoning with what it is to be an American. The great ones consciously wrestle with that.  High Noon. The Searchers. The Man Who Shot Liberty Valance. Yadda yadda. What leaves me cold with Once Upon a Time in the West is I don’t feel that reckoning.  What I feel is that this is a profoundly well-crafted movie that emulates what makes westerns entertaining, and dialing up the craft to a very stylized degree. Like, I dunno man, this sorta feels like how Tarantino approaches moviemaking. You know, taking something he loves and turning the dial to ten. Which I understand why people would like that, it’s undeniably captivating, but to me it tramples over what makes the other thing great. Also, I think Charles Bronson has the charisma of a sock. *I still do, but you get the point

C'era una volta il west. C'era una volta una terra ancora tutta da scoprire, abitata da intraprendenti cacciatori di taglie e temibili banditi. Giunto al quinto lungometraggio Sergio Leone evolve la sua poetica e mette in scena un western crepuscolare, dove la frontiera perde il suo fascino. La pellicola distrugge i vecchi archetipi del genere e si focalizza sulla forza inarrestabile del progresso, rappresentato dal treno a vapore. Dói muito reconhecer que me decepcionei com uma obra do Leone. Sua trilogia dos dólares é provavelmente minha trilogia favorita do cinema, o terceiro filme estando entre meus top 10 filmes da vida. No entanto, este filme, com todo respeito, é uma versão reduzida de The Good, the Bad and the Ugly , no sentido da exploração da moralidade de personagens, definidos pelas suas ambiguidades. O que torna o filme mencionado incrível é a sua execução tão primorosa de histórias simples em minha visão, que são engrandecidas pelos close-ups, diálogos marcantes, e a dinâmica dos personagens entre si, entre outros fatores. Só que no caso de Once Upon a Time in the West , eu não vejo algumas dessas qualidades. Aqui, Leone diverge de um dos meus pontos favoritos de seus filmes: suas tomadas longas que nunca são apenas suficientes, mas também que nunca se excedem. Basicamente ele tirava máximo proveito de cada plano de seus filmes, proporcionando uma experiência lenta mas cadenciada, T.G.B.U., por exemplo, mesmo com suas 3 horas na versão estendida, foi provavelmente o filme com as 3 horas mais fluídas que já vi. Sendo sincero, esse foi o maior problema que tive com o filme. Achei extremamente arrastado. Eu entendo que o filme possui um tom certamente fúnebre, elegíaco, por causa da modernização do velho oeste pelo advento da ferrovia por exemplo, algo que eu acho muito interessante. A própria personagem da Jill engloba bastante esse fator e por esse e outros motivos, como sua história de superação, o que acabou se tornando minha favorita do filme. Os outros personagens principais, no entanto, não acho que são escritos tão bem. Frank e especialmente Cheyenne achei fracos, possuem um desenvolvimento rushado que afeta até o próprio confronto final. Falando sobre ele, sinceramente, acho que é a pior cena de climax/final que o Leone fez até agora dos filmes que vi dele. É apressada e mal filmada. Também achei a inserção do flashback do Harmonica inorgânica e confusa. Toda a montagem do confronto é precária na minha visão. Mas, pra não parecer que eu odeio o filme, ele tem fortes pontos positivos. Pontos chave de obras do Leone, em grande parte da rodagem, estão presentes. Os cenários, a trilha sonora marcante, os diálogos, as cenas de confronto (exceto a final), os close-ups, etc. Concluindo, adianto que um dia verei novamente o filme. Respeito muito o Leone, a forma como ele reproduz o velho oeste em seus filmes, é marcante e, especialmente, acessível. Vendo seu primeiro filme do gênero me deixou muito interessado pelo tema, não a toa rapidamente vi os outros dois da trilogia e fiquei apaixonado. Não é um filme nota 6 de um diretor qualquer. Mas, ainda assim, não consigo esconder o que eu senti vendo... Uma pena.

I’m disappointed. Certainly not bad, just not what I was hoping for, I guess. It’s got Morricone cooking up pure excellence, epic close-ups with Leone’s brilliant filmmaking, vast landscapes, but there is something absent here. It almost feels like he wanted this to be his ultimate western—a story of modern civilization and a dying age of outlaws. Characters driven by the future, the past—some lost in a world that seems to be moving on without them. From the start, I don’t think I ever latched on; I never boarded the train. I don’t think I wanted to leave. Coming in, I guess I expected an energetic story, full of stupid excitement through sweaty men chasing greed and betraying each other left and right—something I thought would eventually come in the movie. The characters reflect the pacing; it’s purposefully slow, with characters staring at each other for five minutes before they say a word. Usually, I don’t mind the drawn-out sequences that Sergio Leone utilizes—but here, it was almost taking me out of the experience. It still has that same gritty atmosphere that I enjoy, but it switches up its tone to represent a dying age of outlaws; a theme I don’t think I ever truly realized. It’s probably my own fault, because at times I felt I failed to make sense of certain characters’ purposes—like Jill. After researching, I understand the context, but I definitely failed to understand that on this initial watch. Typically, Leone gives you just enough to understand a character or a situation, a clue I think almost misguided me throughout my viewing. I felt myself slipping as the story progressed, turning farther and farther away until I almost became lost in my head; I couldn’t comprehend what Leone was trying to convey. The movie trades the flashy, high-octane energy of Duck, You Sucker! and the Dollars Trilogy for pure subtlety—a choice that completely alters the experience tenfold. If I had gotten some sort of a heads-up on what to expect, I might have appreciated this way more, like I wish I could. Great performances—none of them being my absolute favorite from a Leone film, but solid all around. Technically, it's a masterpiece, but I felt completely detached from the story. What makes it tough is that the plot feels like the main focus here, unlike Leone's other, more style-driven Spaghetti Westerns. 6.3/10

I'm beginning to realize I like these films because I like watching Clint Eastwood... moreso than because I like watching a Sergio Leone film. Blasphemous, I know. But it's why I don't think I liked this film very much. Charles Bronson does a fine job as Harmonica, but he ain't no Clint Eastwood. I'm just not quite immersed watching a film with characters I'm not particularly interested in. It's especially infuriating since this could all be fixed with slightly more defining characterization. The characters are on the brink of being interesting, be it Jill's reliance on men as an inherent survival instinct, or Frank's struggle to adapt to the modern world quickly moving away from the primative laws of the old west, the core idea of the characters are there but they are never fully explored. The film just spends majority of the runtime flexing Sergio Leone's style, which means every scene feels like slow and sluggish build up that has no proper payoff. Alot of people can stomach the slower pace, but not me. I think things move along way too slowly for me to really appreciate the ideas they're going for because it's spread so thinly across a  three hour runtime. For me, there's too little story beats to properly flesh out the narrative. I don't think it helps that the past few Sergio Leone westerns I've seen are never quite as epic as you'd want them to be. There's the amazing soundtrack playing in the background sure, but the weight of the moment was really lost on me this time around. Like I said, I really do think the payoff needs to be a little more grand to justify the slow build up, and this is just not enough for me. Honestly, the music by Ennio Morricone might be the one thing that's consistently excellent throughout all these films. There's just such a distinct sound to these films that makes every moment a little easier to sit through. Although... I think I still prefer the soundtrack from A Few Dollars More over this. And I can't deny how beautiful Sergio Leone's films look. Especially in this one, there's incredible density in these spaces and set designs unlike anything in his previous films that just brings the town to life. It feels like a lived in town, unlike some of the sets in the Dollar Trilogy which feel completely desolate even though it's supposed to be a living breathing community space. The film is also... really well lit. Like really really well lit. Anyways, I'm really not that big a fan of Sergio Leone. Unfortunate.

But, obviously, the scene-stealer in this whole movie is Henry Fonda.  His icy blue eyes and his weather-beaten face are just perfect for this role. This is a fantastic movie that will stay with me for a while.  Possibly my favorite of Leone's.

I didn't like this much on the first watch; I enjoyed Leone's visual side, some really great camera framing, and the performances, but I couldn't get into what I thought was a long, overdrawn story. On a rewatch, I did quite love it, even if I think its story is certainly pushed to its limits, but that Sergio Leone visual style is so heavily awesome here in terms of its complete control of his operative visual storytelling, elevating his story to mythic levels. Even the smallest moments have such a strong visual side, making the smallest of gestures hold such emotional weight, and that final climax between Bronson and Fonda is one of the greatest camera-framing scenes out there and it's just so cool. Leone seems to linger on the idea of violence a lot here, and the never-ending build-up, when it does eventually explode into sudden violence, somehow feels just as meticulous and controlled. Even if I think the story is a tad bit too long, it reaches this really fun level of watching Leone frame every shot against his really beautiful cinematography, and all the scenes featuring Ennio Morricone's score are truly masterful. What a score that really is, and how it underscores most of this film and becomes such an integral part of its filmmaking itself. Every bit of emotional scoring and character themes give it that broader sense of richness and adds to that mythology, and it even adds a strong sense of melancholy to the smaller scenes, even if it revels in the larger moments here. This one also differs from his Dollars trilogy in the way its climax of the old West comes into play so heavily throughout. The arrival of the railroad represents the encroachment of industrialization and modernity, gradually rendering the gunslingers, outlaws, and frontier mythology obsolete. It is very focused on that transition between violence and the uncertain future approaching the West, and even all our characters are relics of the past, but even so, Leone still blends that romantic mythology of the West with its ruthless economic interests shaping the future, creating an interesting angle. It is quite top-tier in all respects as a Western, and as a requiem for the Western genre, it is quite excellent; just how much it simultaneously celebrates the conventions of the genre while bringing Leone's own touch is phenomenal. I have to mention those awesome Bronson and Robards performances and the ever-beautiful Cardinale on full show here too. I'm glad I checked it out again, though, and got such extra richness from it, and I'm planning to rewatch Duck, You Sucker! next, which seems to remain an underrated film of Leone's.

Hey Harmonica - when they do you in, pray it's someone who knows where to shoot... - Cheyenne Directed by the supreme father of spaghetti western - with a story co-written alongside two other great italian directors (Dario Argento and Bernardo Bertolucci), with wonderful and suggestive scenarios and a magnificent score by Ennio Morricone - Once Upon a Time in the West continues to captivate its audience even after almost 60 years from its release. It does so through masterful cinematography that immerse the viewer in the Wild West - an arid, harsh world that both gives to and takes from its inhabitants - and by delving into the characters' psyches (particularly through extreme close-ups). The film also employs suspense so skillfully crafted that it keeps you on the seat even during sequences where, theoretically, no violence occurs (ex. such the introduction scene of Ceyenne) and the effective use of long takes father enhances the sense of being right there among the characters in that very moment  (eg. Jill's arrival at the station and the final showdown). Beyond their multifaced psychology, the characters are essentially archetypes in a modern fairy tale set in the Old West; each embodies a specific type of coloners struggling to survive and prosperity. They range from Jill (played by Claudia Cardinale), who seeks her fortune going from the city to the desert without exploiting others or being exploited herself, to Frank and Morton - who from their respective positions, represent the sharks of that world, ruthless in their pursuit of profit and power - and Cheyenne (my personal favorite), the rough outlaw with a human heart. The only sorta of exception in this regard is Harmonica, played by Charles Bronson, who functions more as a solitary "spectre" of vengeance - a dead man driven solely by revenge, yet still possessing glitters of humanity beneath his calm and seemingly unreadable gaze and the sound of his harmonica, which becomes an omen of death for others.

Some movies are all style over substance, but this movie combines both to create a fucking masterpiece. I want to start by saying: whoa, this is so entertaining! For almost three hours, there isn't a single scene that feels too long, and that's incredible. The acting is unbelievable. Every performance is perfect, and thanks to that, the characters are incredibly deep. Of course, the main villain, played by Fonda, is absolutely perfect. The story of a legendary man known as Harmonica is a great idea. It makes you feel that something important is going to happen and that the entire movie is building towards something. Sometimes it's the direction, sometimes it's the music, and sometimes it's something else entirely. So, just like its title suggests, the movie is truly a fairy tale, but set in the American West. And that's what makes it so good, because we know that the final line isn't going to be 'and they got married and had lots of children'. It's going to be something much deeper, and that ending is perfect. The best thing about this movie is Leone's direction. Every frame leaves an impression. There are so many scenes that perfectly demonstrate the 'show, don't tell' approach, and wow, I love that. Of course, Leone is known for his long, contemplative scenes, which leave you speechless because of their quality. The sets and cinematography are so beautiful. Every shot feels like a fairy tale, but a dirty one, and that's what makes it so beautiful. Every frame looks like a painting, but this painting is a masterpiece. Alongside the cinematography, the dirty colour palette makes you feel as if you've lived alongside the characters and experienced their story. The script is also fantastic. There are so many moments that make you feel surprised, angry, sad, happy and deeply touched. The soundtrack is a beautiful element that accompanies every shot, giving it a new meaning. That's the magic of the soundtracks in Leone's movies. So, when I watched this movie, just like The Good, the Bad and the Ugly, I felt like I was in the Wild West for almost three hours. And those were some of the best hours of my life. Sergio Leone is simply incredible when it comes to spaghetti westerns. I love this experience, which makes you feel like you're a cool, lonely cowboy in a vast Western landscape. 🤠🤑💥

I was really nervous I was going to hate this movie going in, since I wasn’t a huge fan of Leone’s Once Upon A Time in America and found A Fistful of Dollars to be solid but not extraordinary, but I found this film to be much more in line with something like Leone’s The Good, The Bad, and the Ugly which I am a big fan of. The four leads are all compelling and interesting in their own ways. For me the least interesting of the four is Claudia Cardinale as the widow Jill, despite a strong performance her character just isn’t given the same attention as the others. Henry Fonda gives a killer performance as the vile outlaw Frank and has some incredible moments (one of my favorite scenes from the film is when he and his band of outlaws kill the family), Charles Bronson is solid as the silent revenge fueled Harmonica but I wasn’t a massive fan of his character, and Jason Robards gives a surprisingly fun performance as the outlaw with a heart of gold, Cheyenne, who quickly became one of my favorite characters. Each character brings a different part of the western mythos to this film and create interesting dichotomies of society vs freedom, money vs morals, violence and revenge, physical power vs financial power, among others. The movie looks absolutely beautiful, this has to be some of the best cinematography in film. The movie could have been shorter but then there wouldn’t have been the insane amount of sick shots when every character needs 45 seconds to aura farm before doing anything. One of the things that no other western director has ever really captured is how cool everyone looks in Leone westerns. And of course Ennio Morricone creates another incredible soundtrack, Morricone is probably my favorite film composer of all time.

retrato de um gênero, retrato de um oeste e do faroeste, retrato da figura do cowboy, retrato de um país que nasce dentro das dicotomias entre o certo e o errado, o bem e o mal, sem perceber que todas essas faces se misturam e se entrelaçam na tentativa de sobrevivência em um ambiente que finca suas raízes e estabelece sua base na violência. leone não apenas percebe isso, como retrata magistralmente todas essas contradições. uma verdadeira aula de cinema, que conta uma história sem pressa, construindo uma trama sólida, com cenas e sequências que transitam do olhar mais íntimo dos personagens aos planos abertos do ambiente em que se encontram. tudo acontece nas minúcias; o filme se conta por si só, sem medo de mostrar, de revelar ao telespectador, de transferir sua atmosfera e de tensionar cada ambiente. a tensão é fundamental, mergulhando a audiência naquele espaço que preenche os olhos de quem assiste e faz pulsar o coração de quem sente cada movimento, cada cálculo que constitui a cena e o filme como um todo. uma das reviravoltas mais impactantes da história do cinema e um exemplo de como tornar um filme inesquecível. o som da gaita vai tocar para sempre na minha cabeça. o arquétipo da vingança, a construção precisa de cada personagem é sempre um deleite de se ver. apesar de todos os elogios, acredito que o meu maior deles, e o aspecto que mais admiro, é a forma como leone faz de jill a protagonista absoluta do filme. a única personagem feminina, que poderia facilmente ser reduzida a nada ou a um mero objeto de motivação para o herói. acontece justamente o contrário e ela se revela como a peça fundamental que move toda a trama ao transformar sua tragédia em força e utilizar todas as artimanhas possíveis para sobreviver em um ambiente dominado por homens que sequer a enxergam e, ainda assim, consegue vencer todos eles. o futuro do filme é feminino, assim como maria firmina dos reis propôs em seu romance "úrsula" . a narrativa expõe que, enquanto a masculinidade produz todos os descontroles da sociedade — algo que vemos perfeitamente ao longo do filme —, é a figura feminina que surge como a harmonia capaz de superar esses eventos catastróficos, exatamente como nos mostram não apenas a cena final, mas toda a sequência de encerramento. a tríade de protagonistas masculinos encara, de forma árdua, o destino de suas próprias façanhas, enquanto a única personagem feminina alcança um desfecho feliz e próspero, sem precisar estar vinculada a um relacionamento amoroso, a um casamento ou a uma figura masculina que conduza sua jornada. ela escapa do destino que lhe parecia reservado e consegue transformar o ambiente repressor que ali estava estabelecido. esse último parágrafo toma como inspiração os meus estudos e apenas estabelece uma relação com a ficção da obra cinematográfica. nenhuma das ideias apresentadas é originalmente minha e elas foram mobilizadas apenas para dialogar com o contexto fílmico desta obra-prima do cinema.
